newsitem.title: INDIA: Reliance starts work on India's biggest refinery.
newsitem.headline: Reliance starts work on India's biggest refinery.

text.p: India's Reliance Petroleum has started work on the country's largest, and one of the world's biggest refineries, confident that it will remain profitable despite federal plans to deregulate the industry.
There is hectic activity at the site of the 300,000 barrel- per-day refinery near the port town of Jamnagar on India's west coast, Reliance officials told Reuters on Tuesday.
"Bechtel has already started award of contracts for major process facilities," a Reliance spokesman said.
Bechtel Group Inc of the U.S., an engineering, development, construction and project management giant, has sole responsibility for completion of the project.
The 86.94 billion rupee ($2.44 billion) refinery is expected to be commissioned in the year 2000.
By then, analysts said, India will have given up its administered pricing regime for petroleum products.

The federal government now regulates prices of petroleum products and refiners are assured a 12 percent return on net worth. The government has said it intends to deregulate the industry and remove state subsidies but has not indicated when.
Some analysts said this could affect the profitability and viability of the Reliance refinery.
"A refinery at today's international margins won't be viable whatever the size," said an oil analyst at a research firm.

Analysts at an oil conference in Singapore on Monday said refining profit margins in Asia are expected to remain narrow in the next five years, making it difficult to justify new grassroots investments.
Refining margins fell steadily in Asia from the 1990/1991 Gulf War to a 10-year low in 1995.
But Reliance officials said they anticipated no problems.

"We will be able to compete successfully with other refineries even in a decontrolled environment due to economies of scale, ability to process varied types of crude, a process configuration for maximising production of light and middle distillates to achieve higher refining margins," the Reliance spokesman said.
Another positive factor would be captive demand for some of the refinery's products from the petrochemical and power projects of the Reliance group of firms, the company said.
Over 20 percent of the refinery output, valued at around $582 million annually of a total $2.9 billion, will be consumed by Reliance Industries, India's largest private firm.
In fiscal 1995/96 (April to March), India's petroleum products consumption rose to 75.4 million tonnes, up almost 11 percent from the previous year.
The government has projected India's demand for petroleum products will reach 113 million tonnes by 2000/2001.
The independent Centre for Monitoring the Indian Economy (CMIE), said eight refinery projects, including Reliance, would add 46 million tonnes of new refining capacity by 1999/2000.
The refinery's naphtha will be a feedstock for Reliance Industries's petrochemical operations, and petroleum coke would be used to fire the group's proposed power plants.

"Size and downstream integration are key areas," said Avdhoot Sabnis, analyst at brokerage James Capel B&K. "They (Reliance) would be better off than others," he said, referring to new refineries planned by other business houses.
But the oil analyst at the research firm said new refiners are bound to get tariff protection, without which no new refineries would be built in India.
